title: App size, static vs dynamic linking
summary: Static libraries are copied into your app binary (faster launch, unused code removed). Dynamic frameworks are loaded at launch (can be shared with extensions, but slower launch). Default to static.
body: **In simple words:** **Static** linking glues library code into your app at build time. **Dynamic** linking keeps it as a separate framework that is loaded when the app starts.

**Trade-offs:** static = faster launch and dead-code stripping, but code used by app and extensions is duplicated. Dynamic = shared between app and extensions, but each framework adds launch time. Mergeable libraries (Xcode 15+) are dynamic in debug (fast builds) and merged statically in release.
**Gotcha:** linking the same static library into two dynamic frameworks puts two copies in the app - bigger size and possible "class implemented in both" runtime warnings.

**Reducing app size:** asset catalogs (App Store thins per device), compress/stream large media, on-demand resources, remove unused code and assets, audit third-party SDKs (often the biggest), strip debug symbols, consider `-Osize` where performance allows.
**Why size matters:** large downloads reduce install conversion, especially on cellular; there is a cellular download size prompt.
**Staff angle:** track download/install size per build (App Store Connect size reports, app thinning report) and fail CI on unexpected growth.
keyPoints: Static = faster launch, stripped; dynamic = shareable with extensions, launch cost.
Default SPM packages to static; dynamic only for sharing with extensions.
Mergeable libraries give dynamic debug + static release.
Biggest size wins: assets, third-party SDKs, unused code.
Track size per build and alert on growth.

code.caption: SPM product types
code.text:
products: [
    .library(name: "DesignSystem", targets: ["DesignSystem"]),          // automatic (usually static)
    .library(name: "SharedKit", type: .dynamic, targets: ["SharedKit"]) // shared by app + extensions
]

followups: **How do generics affect size?** Specialization creates copies of generic code per concrete type, which can grow the binary.
